title: Columbus Diocese Plans to Demolish 1908 Gay St. Building
author: CRE News Staff
excerpt: The Diocese of Columbus filed to demolish its 1908 building at 197 E. Gay St. for surface parking. The Downtown Commission votes September 22, 2026.

body:
The Roman Catholic Diocese of Columbus filed a Certificate of Appropriateness with the city's Planning Division to demolish its 1908 five-story building at 197 East Gay Street and convert the site to surface parking. The Downtown Commission, which must approve demolition in the historic district, is scheduled to take up the application on September 22.

## What the Diocese Submitted

A Certificate of Appropriateness is the permit Columbus requires before anyone alters or demolishes a building within the Downtown Commission's jurisdiction, which covers exterior changes, new construction, and demolition in the downtown core. The application describes the project scope as demolition of the building and its "conversion to surface parking," according to [Columbus Underground](https://columbusunderground.com/church-wants-to-tear-down-5-story-downtown-building-bw1/), which reported the filing on September 2. The filing was made with the Planning Division; no demolition permit has been pulled with the city's Building and Zoning Services as of publication.

The Diocese has not released a public statement on the application. CREN sought comment from the Diocese of Columbus; no response had been received by publication time.

## The Building and Its Tenants

The building at 197 East Gay Street was constructed in 1908 and is five stories. The Diocese has owned it since the 1960s, and it currently houses three occupants: the Diocese's administrative offices, Catholic Social Services of the Diocese of Columbus, and the Our Lady of Guadalupe Center, which provides pastoral and social services to Columbus's Latino Catholic community.

The Diocese has not announced relocation plans for any of the three tenants. No timeline for vacating the building has appeared in the public filing or in Diocese communications reviewed as of this writing. Catholic Social Services and the Our Lady of Guadalupe Center both provide programs whose continuity is relevant to the communities they serve, and where those programs would relocate is not addressed in the submitted application.

## Location in the Cathedral Block

The building sits in one of the more intact early-twentieth-century institutional blocks remaining in downtown Columbus. It stands behind [Saint Joseph Cathedral](https://www.stjosephcathedral.net/) at 212 E. Broad Street, next door to the [Columbus Athenaeum](https://www.columbusathenaeum.com/) at 32 N. 4th Street — a historic events venue still in active use — and across E. Gay Street from condominium units developed by Edwards Companies under its Neighborhood Launch initiative.

The [Catholic Diocese of Columbus](https://columbuscatholic.org/venue/197-e-gay-st-parking-lot/) lists a "197 E. Gay St. Parking Lot" as a venue on its website, indicating some existing parking use at the address. The relationship between that existing use and the building the Diocese seeks to demolish is not specified in publicly available documents.

## Why the Building Is in Trouble

An unsafe order was placed on the structure after a brick wall collapsed in January 2026. The Diocese has not released a structural assessment or estimates for repairs. The unsafe order is the disclosed precipitating event, though it does not by itself authorize demolition — the Certificate of Appropriateness process and Downtown Commission approval remain required regardless of building condition.

Historically, the Downtown Commission has weighed demolition applications against the applicant's documentation of condition and repair costs, the building's significance within the historic district, and whether adaptive reuse or rehabilitation is feasible. When owners have demonstrated that rehabilitation costs exceed a building's viable economic use, the Commission has sometimes permitted demolition to proceed. When the record is thin or alternatives appear viable, the Commission has requested additional documentation or required alternatives. The Diocese's case will likely turn on what condition evidence and cost estimates it presents at the hearing.

## The Surface Parking Tension

This application arrives while Columbus is running a 60-day public comment period on Zone In Phase 2, the city's comprehensive [zoning code modernization](https://columbusrealestatenews.com/blog/columbus-zone-in-phase-2-public-comment) that opened August 25 and extends through October 24. Zone In Phase 2 is specifically designed to add density and reduce surface parking's footprint in the city's urban core.

Replacing a five-story building with a surface lot would move counter to that direction on a block that sits within the walkable, transit-proximate downtown core that both Zone In and the city's long-range comprehensive plan identify as a priority for active-use development. That tension between an institutional property owner's decision and city planning goals is one the Downtown Commission will need to navigate. The Commission's mandate is historic preservation, not land-use planning, but surface parking conversion of a historic building is precisely the scenario that Columbus's Certificate of Appropriateness process was designed to give the Commission authority to weigh.

The Columbus Athenaeum, immediately adjacent, would be a logical party to weigh in; no public statement from the Athenaeum had been released as of publication. The Columbus Preservation Office advises the Commission on historic resource significance; its assessment of the property has not been made public.

## What to Watch

If the Diocese's application is on the agenda — which has not been formally published as of this writing — the Commission will take public comment before voting to approve, deny, or table the demolition request. An approval allows the Diocese to proceed to a demolition permit; a denial requires the Diocese to either appeal or revise its approach.

The building's fate after any Commission decision would depend on whether the Diocese pursues demolition, explores sale or adaptive reuse, or undertakes emergency stabilization of the structure pending a longer-term plan. None of those paths has been announced.
